title: What is a virtual receptionist? Types, costs, and how they work
summary: A virtual receptionist answers your business calls remotely, using either a live person or AI. Compare the three types, what each costs, and which fits your business.
body_markdown:
Your business is growing, and the phone is ringing off the hook. If your team is missing calls, you’re losing out on potential sales.


A virtual receptionist answers your business calls remotely, using either a live person or an AI voice agent built into your phone system. It handles the same front-desk work an in-house receptionist would: greeting callers, answering common questions, routing calls, taking messages, and booking appointments.


A human virtual receptionist can better handle complicated calls, but costs $200 to $3,000 per month. An AI receptionist is better for basic calls, but gives you instant pickup at any hour, and costs $25 to $200+ per month. Most businesses run both: AI catches the overflow and the after-hours calls, and a person handles escalations.


In this guide, we’ll cover the costs and benefits of different types of virtual receptionists so you can choose the right option for your business.


##


What is a virtual receptionist?


A[virtual receptionist](https://www.quo.com/product/virtual-receptionist) answers the phone and handles simple tasks after hours or when your team is busy. The term may be confusing because it covers both human and AI tools that work remotely or through a software system, rather than in-house like traditional receptionists.


### What does a virtual receptionist do?


Hiring a virtual receptionist or using an[automated receptionist](https://www.quo.com/blog/automated-receptionist/) takes many tasks off your team’s plate, including:


- Screening spam and telemarketing calls since they can’t answer the virtual receptionist’s questions
- Message taking during or after hours
- Routing calls to the right departments
- Capturing and saving customer details
- Scheduling appointments
- Processing or assisting with orders
- Taking payments or updating payment information
- Answering FAQs
- Providing basic customer service
- Offering bilingual services


With this extra help, you don’t have to worry about missing calls or losing leads, even with[high call volume](https://www.quo.com/blog/high-call-volume/) .

Let’s take a look at these options in detail.


### 1. AI voice agents built into virtual phone systems


Some phone communication software comes with a built-in AI voice agent, such as Quo’s Sona. An AI receptionist like Sona is a cost-effective way to ensure calls are answered 24/7. Urgent calls are transferred to the right person, and details are captured directly into your business phone system for quick follow-up. Sona can also[send SMS for lead capture](https://www.quo.com/sona#leads-over-sms) .


A built-in option like Sona is useful if you want a comprehensive phone system to handle increased call volumes as your business grows. You[can try Sona out for free](https://my.quo.com/signup) for seven days — it takes just minutes to get started.


**Related:** ****** Compare the[best AI phone answering services](https://www.quo.com/blog/best-ai-phone-answering-services/) for your business to see how Sona stacks up.


### 2. Third-party AI voice agents that integrate with virtual phone systems


If your current communication software doesn’t offer a remote receptionist, you can add a standalone AI agent. These third-party[voice agents](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/voice-agent) integrate with your existing phone system through call forwarding.


When incoming calls are forwarded to the AI answering service, it makes it difficult to maintain oversight. Conversations live in different apps, so your team will have to spend extra time switching between platforms to find important details.


### 3. Traditional human-powered virtual receptionist services


Hiring a real receptionist gives you a person to answer calls and do things like plan appointments, process payments, and take in new clients. They can also filter calls and qualify leads to save your team time.


But there are trade-offs. Human remote receptionists cost more and take longer to onboard than AI solutions. Also, many services only send call details by email or text, not directly into your CRM.


A good solution is using both AI and human virtual receptionists. ER Fukuda, CEO and Co-Founder of Rainbow Road Transport, said:


*“We used Quo for incoming calls, with live agents answering calls directly. This worked well during business hours, but we struggled to manage the overflow. Sona has been instrumental in filling those gaps. It collects key information from the caller, so when our agents return in the morning, they have a queue of qualified leads to process, which speeds up our response time and improves booking conversion.”*


##


What a virtual receptionist is not: Comparing common alternatives


Virtual receptionists go by many names — call answering services, auto-attendants, virtual assistants — but each type serves different needs. Here’s the breakdown:


System What it does Availability Handles complex requests? Human interaction?


In-house receptionist Handles calls plus in-person walk-ins and appointments Business hours, one location Yes Yes — in person


Answering service (call center) Takes messages and forwards calls at high volume Often 24/7 Limited Yes, but less personalized


Auto-attendant Fixed phone menu; routes calls by keypad ("press 1") 24/7 No — routing only No


IVR Menu by keypad or voice; some self-service for balances, payments 24/7 No — basic tasks only No


Virtual assistant Phone plus broader tasks (projects, travel, bookkeeping) Varies Yes Yes


### Virtual receptionist vs in-house receptionist


**


Traditional receptionists are there to handle walk-in customers or appointments in person. But some drawbacks mean they’re not right for every business:


- **Cost:** Traditional receptionists cost more than virtual ones and require investing in in-office equipment.
- **Flexibility:** Front desk receptionists can only work during business hours, whereas virtual help can answer the phone and provide solutions 24/7.
- **Limited location** : In-house staff establish a human presence for local businesses, but they’re limited to one area or region. Virtual receptionists can work remotely from anywhere and serve customers around the world.


### Virtual receptionist vs answering service call centers


**


A virtual[answering service](https://www.quo.com/answering-service) based in a call center typically offers limited, basic help, like taking messages and forwarding calls. Because they focus on efficiency and volume, answering service call centers may not feel as personalized or friendly as virtual receptionists. They may also require more training to handle[screening calls as a receptionist](https://www.quo.com/blog/screening-calls-receptionist/) .


**💡Related:** Is an answering service better than voicemail? Find out here:[Voicemail vs answering service](https://www.quo.com/blog/voicemail-vs-answering-service/)


### Virtual receptionist vs auto-attendants vs IVR


**


An auto-attendant and[IVR](https://www.quo.com/blog/what-is-ivr/) answer and route calls automatically, but they’re different systems.


- An auto-attendant is a fixed[phone menu.](https://www.quo.com/blog/phone-menu/) Callers hear a set list of options and press a number to get where they’re going. There’s no AI or speech recognition behind it.
- An interactive voice response is a digital system that automatically routes calls when customers press a number or say an option. Some IVR systems can handle simple self-service tasks on their own, like checking an account balance or taking a payment.


The difference between a[virtual receptionist vs automated answering](https://www.quo.com/blog/virtual-receptionist-vs-automated-answering-service/) is that receptionists can handle complex requests. Auto-attendants and IVRs can only give basic information and do call transfers to make call handling more efficient for your receptionist or team.


### Virtual receptionist vs virtual assistant


**


A virtual *receptionist* focuses on answering calls and providing customer service.


A virtual *assistant* does more than just answer the phone. They can do things like manage projects, plan trips, and do basic administrative tasks.

##


Is a live virtual receptionist worth it?


Consider some of the benefits you get when you invest in a human receptionist or AI voice agent:


- [Never miss a call](https://www.quo.com/product/call-management/never-miss-a-call) **again.** With 24/7 availability, virtual receptionist services can answer calls after hours, on weekends, and on holidays. And you’ll always have someone available to cover for employees when they call in sick or go on vacation.
- **Cost-effective solution for growing businesses.** Hiring an in-house receptionist can cost[around $41,000 per year](https://www.salary.com/research/salary/benchmark/receptionist-i-salary) when you factor in benefits and bonuses. Virtual receptionists offer flexible monthly pricing to meet changing needs.
- **Scale up or down based on demand.** You can easily scale up or reduce virtual receptionist services as your business grows or has seasonal changes in customer inquiries. This means you don’t have to hire temporary onsite help.
- **Flexible service tailored to your business.** Both human and AI receptionists can use custom scripts and call handling preferences to give customers a consistent, professional experience. Some services also let you add options like outbound calling as your business needs change.
- **Professional service without the overhead.** Human virtual receptionists likely have customer service skills and don’t require expensive training or weeks of paid onboarding. An AI agent can be even more cost-effective because it needs only a few minutes of setup to start providing[missed call services](https://www.quo.com/features/missed-call-service) .


Here’s what one customer said:


*“Prior to adopting Sona, we struggled with consistently capturing after-hours communications, resulting in missed opportunities. We now have absolute assurance that every incoming call is handled promptly.”* Jon Christensen, Co-founder, Bidmii


##


How much does a virtual receptionist cost?


Using an AI[voice receptionist costs](https://www.quo.com/blog/virtual-receptionist-cost/) from $25 to over $200 per month. Pricing depends on the number of minutes or calls you need and includes features like integrations and bilingual support. Quo’s Sona is available on tiered, usage-based plans that start at $25 per month — and you get 10 free monthly calls on every plan.


Human receptionists typically cost much more, from $200 to over $3,000 per month. Some services offer less-expensive basic packages, but you may not get features like appointment scheduling or basic customer service.

4. Connect your calendar, CRM, business phone, and other tools.
5. Test a few calls and adjust as needed before rolling it out to your customers.

##


Verdict: Which type of virtual receptionist should you choose?


Most small businesses don’t need to choose between a person and software. They need to stop missing calls.


If your calls are mostly routine, arrive outside business hours, or come in faster than your team can pick up, an AI receptionist built into your business phone system is the cheapest way to catch them. Platforms like Quo include AI answering on every plan.


If your calls are high-value, emotionally loaded, or need real judgment, pay for a human service and route only those calls to it.


Running both human and AI receptionists is usually cheaper than staffing a front desk, and it’s the setup most growing businesses land on.


##


FAQs


****How does a virtual receptionist work?****


With a virtual receptionist, incoming calls to your business number are routed to a human or AI agent. The receptionist answers using your personalized greeting and handles the call according to your instructions. This can include taking messages, answering questions, transferring calls, or collecting leads for follow-up.


****How do virtual receptionists enhance the customer experience?****


Using a virtual receptionist ensures that customers always reach a real person or helpful AI agent, even after hours. With professional, consistent 24/7 service, customers always get assistance rather than a busy signal or generic voicemail message.


****What types of businesses use virtual receptionists?****


Your business could benefit from human or[AI receptionists](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/receptionist) if:


– You’re missing lots of calls due to high call volume
– You’re growing and want the advantage of 24/7 phone coverage
– You have a global customer base
– You provide professional services, run an independent practice, or sell products online


****Which businesses don’t need a virtual receptionist?****


You might not need to invest in a virtual receptionist if your business is brand new, has very low call volume, or mainly deals with local customers who call during standard business hours.


**Is a virtual receptionist worth it for a small business?**


Yes, especially for after-hours coverage, since[74% of consumers](https://cxtrends.zendesk.com/gb) expect customer service to be available 24/7. The options are usually voicemail, a forwarded cell phone, or nothing. A virtual receptionist prevents customers from reaching dead ends.
The practical setup looks like this: the receptionist answers, works out why the person is calling, and either captures the details for morning follow-up or routes the call straight to whoever is on call. That way, you never miss a call or opportunity.


**What skills does a virtual receptionist need?**


Professional phone communication, comfort with call routing and scheduling software, organization under interruption, and the judgment to know when a call needs escalating rather than a message taken.


For AI receptionists, the equivalent is how well the system is trained on your business: the quality of the answers depends on the quality of the information you give it.


**How do I write a script for a virtual receptionist?**


Cover three things: a greeting that names your business, the questions you need answered on every call, and clear instructions for what happens next, whether that’s booking, routing, or taking a message. Keep it short. Long scripts make callers wait and make AI agents sound robotic.
